faq.a: Look for growth at 42 °C, resistance to fluconazole, and persistent colonisation of skin sites; a simple CHROMagar may hint at C. auris.
faq.q: How can I differentiate C. auris from other yeasts without advanced labs?

faq.a: If the patient is critically ill, the isolate is carbapenem‑resistant, and meropenem MIC is > 4 µg/mL, add colistin early.
faq.q: When should I add colistin for a suspected CRE infection?

faq.a: Eliminate standing water, use indoor residual spraying, and provide insecticide‑treated nets to patients and staff.
faq.q: What vector control measures reduce RVV transmission?

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer with fever, arthralgia, and thrombocytopenia in a rainy season – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Consider RVV; obtain rapid antigen test or use epidemiologic criteria if unavailable.

A neonate in NICU develops candidemia unresponsive to fluconazole – which organism is most likely and what drug do you start? — Suspect C. auris; start an echinocandin because of high fluconazole resistance.

A patient with recent abdominal surgery shows sepsis; cultures grow gram‑negative rods resistant to carbapenems – outline empiric therapy. — Use meropenem plus colistin or tigecycline; avoid carbapenem alone.

During a ward outbreak, bedside cultures are negative but several patients have persistent fever – what infection‑control action is priority? — Reinforce hand hygiene and environmental cleaning; screen staff for C. auris colonisation.

A child presents with hemorrhagic fever signs; RVV test unavailable – which laboratory clues support the diagnosis? — Low platelets, elevated AST/ALT, and high LDH in the context of recent mosquito exposure.

Why is monotherapy with fluconazole inappropriate for suspected invasive candidiasis in a low‑resource African hospital? — High prevalence of C. auris with intrinsic fluconazole resistance; echinocandin offers better coverage.

Explain the rationale for using combination therapy in CRE infections rather than a single agent. — Synergistic killing, prevents emergence of further resistance, and covers heteroresistant subpopulations.

What bedside sign suggests a patient may have a fungal bloodstream infection rather than bacterial? — Persistent, unexplained fever despite 48 h of broad‑spectrum antibiotics, especially with central line presence.
ai.title: Emerging Infectious Diseases 2025
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: A concise guide to the most likely emerging pathogens expected to impact low‑resource African hospitals by 2025, focusing on clinical presentation, diagnosis without advanced labs, and pragmatic management.

b: Focus on pathogens with limited diagnostic capacity.
Prioritise bedside clues and empiric therapy.
sections.p: By 2025 several pathogens are projected to increase in incidence or spread to new regions, driven by climate change, urbanisation and antimicrobial resistance. In East Africa the most clinically relevant are: multidrug‑resistant Gram‑negative bacteria, Candida auris, and arboviruses such as Rift Valley virus (RVV) and emerging flaviviruses.

b: Candida auris – yeast, grows at 42 °C, often misidentified as Candida albicans on routine labs.
Carbapenem‑resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) – gram‑negative rods, produce KPC, NDM, OXA‑48 enzymes.
Rift Valley virus – single‑stranded RNA, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, causes hemorrhagic fever.
sections.p: Each emerging microbe has characteristic morphology and resistance traits that guide empiric choices.

b: C. auris spreads via contaminated surfaces and equipment; persists on dry surfaces for weeks.
CRE spread by patient‑to‑patient contact, contaminated devices, and inadequate hand hygiene.
RVV cycle: mosquito bite → human viremia → mosquito acquisition → new bite.
sections.p: Understanding how these agents spread helps prevent nosocomial outbreaks and community transmission.

b: C. auris – invasive candidemia, urinary tract infection, wound infection; high mortality (> 50 %).
CRE – urinary tract infection, pneumonia, intra‑abdominal sepsis; limited treatment options.
RVV – febrile illness, arthralgia, hemorrhagic diathesis; can progress to shock.
sections.p: Clinical syndromes overlap with common infections, making recognition challenging.
In low‑resource settings rely on bedside patterns and basic labs; when advanced tests are unavailable, use surrogate markers.

t.b: Is the patient bacteremic/fungemic? Positive growth confirms organism; if unavailable, look for persistent fever despite broad antibiotics.

t.a: Gram stain of wound or urine
t.b: Does it show yeast buds (C. auris) or gram‑negative rods (CRE)? Guides empiric coverage.

t.a: Rapid antigen test for RVV (if stocked)
t.b: Is RVV present? Positive test confirms; if not stocked, use epidemiologic link + thrombocytopenia + elevated transaminases.

b: C. auris – start echinocandin (e.g., caspofungin) unless contraindicated; avoid fluconazole due to high resistance.
CRE – use combination therapy: high‑dose meropenem (if MIC ≤ 8 µg/mL) plus colistin or tigecycline; avoid monotherapy with carbapenems alone.
RVV – supportive care; consider ribavirin only in severe cases where available; avoid NSAIDs if bleeding risk.
sections.p: Empiric regimens must cover likely resistant organisms while awaiting confirmation; infection control is essential.

t.b: Is the organism cleared? Persistent positivity signals treatment failure; consider changing regimen.
Are infection‑control practices adequate? Poor compliance predicts outbreak; reinforce with training.
